power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Polyvagal Theory is a systems-level, pathway-specific framework of autonomic regulation developed by Stephen W. Porges, PhD.

Since its formulation in 1994, the theory has profoundly influenced clinical practice by providing a physiological framework for understanding safety, social engagement, and differentiated threat responses.

In January 2026, Paul Grossman and 38 colleagues published a major critique of the theory in Clinical Neuropsychiatry, arguing that important neurophysiological and evolutionary claims of Polyvagal Theory are untenable.

This paper argues that the controversy, as articulated in the current Porges/Grossman debate, and for the last twenty years, has been framed in a way that neither side can resolve because the explanatory variable that would permit adjudication of the central physiological claims of the debate is specified by neither.
The paper proposes a revised physiological model of the living autonomic nervous system that distinguishes neural circuitry from the neurochemical conditions under which that circuitry operates.

Furthermore, it identifies the primary neuromodulatory chemistry required to distinguish between shutdown, emotional freezing, tonic immobility, and dissociation (the states at the centre of the Grossman/Porges dispute) as the family of endogenous opioids: the one family for which a human clinical literature on immobilization already exists, yet a peptide family omitted from the binary two-pole neurochemical model (social buffering and autonomic flexibility: (oxytocin and urocortins), versus vigilance and allostatic load: (vasopressin and corticotropin-releasing hormone)) PVT has endorsed.

With these revisions, observations emphasized by both Porges and Grossman can be understood as accurate relative to the parameters of their descriptions, even though seemingly contradictory, because they are describing different (yet presently unspecified) physiological (neurological and neurochemical) conditions rather than mutually exclusive conclusions.
The model generates new physiological predictions that can be tested experimentally and offers a pathway for resolving a controversy that has remained intractable for two decades.

Independently, the paper establishes the supradiaphragmatic/subdiaphragmatic partition of the vagus on direct human measurement rather than on comparative inference and asserts the importance of this differentiated conduction architecture being an afferent system.
Polyvagal Theory is a systems-level, pathway-specific framework of autonomic regulation developed by Stephen W. Porges, PhD.

Since its formulation in 1994, Polyvagal Theory has profoundly influenced clinical practice by providing a physiological framework for understanding safety, social engagement, and differentiated threat responses.

The theory takes its name from Porges' differentiation of two neuro-anatomically and evolutionarily distinct vagal systems (poly = many, vagal = vagus) that are both parasympathetic and cardio-inhibitory, yet have distinct neuro-anatomical locations in the body, myelination specifications, and biobehavioral function.

This differentiation of two distinct vagal pathways bundled in the common conduit of the vagus nerve updates the neuroanatomical model of autonomic function from a two-term model of autonomic balance (parasympathetic/sympathetic) to a three-term hierarchy (ventral vagal, dorsal vagal, sympathetic) with cascading implications for our understanding of autonomic regulation.

In January 2026, Paul Grossman and 38 colleagues published a major critique of the theory in Clinical Neuropsychiatry, arguing that important neurophysiological and evolutionary claims of Polyvagal Theory are untenable.
"Why The Polyvagal Theory is Untenable: An International Expert Evaluation of the Polyvagal Theory" (2026).
This is not the first critique Grossman has written, but the culmination of a sustained 20-year critique of the theory, the terms of which are largely unmodified since 2007.
Porges responded in the same issue, arguing that the critique does not adequately engage the theory as articulated in the scientific literature.
"When a Critique Becomes Untenable: A Scholarly Response to Grossman et al.'s evaluation of Polyvagal Theory" (2026).

With Grossman's perspective endorsed by 38 vagal experts, the exchange has sharpened a long-standing controversy without resolving its central physiological disagreement, leaving both researchers and clinicians uncertain whether Polyvagal Theory's central ideas a) remain valid because the Grossman et al. critique has missed the mark (Porges' assertion) or b) have now been discredited (Grossman et al.'s assertion), c) remain substantially defensible with modification (Polyvagal Theory needs substantive revision), d) require conceptual or neurophysiological alterations that would fundamentally alter their character (Polyvagal Theory is superseded because revision is so major it represents a novel theoretical formulation), or e) whether Polyvagal Theory should be regarded as a metaphor.

This exchange has produced neither productive field-advancing creative friction nor refined testable theses on either side, but has rather further entrenched a pattern that amplifies a generally unsettled stasis in both the research and clinical domains.

This paper argues that the controversy, as articulated in the current Porges/ Grossman debate, and for the last twenty years, has been framed in a way that neither side can resolve because the explanatory variable that would permit adjudication of the central physiological claims of the debate is specified by neither.
Polyvagal Theory has made the required observation without raising it to a principle.

In 2001 Porges paired an oxytocin-conditioned account of calm immobilization with a vasopressin-conditioned account of immobilized fear at identical dorsal vagal anatomy -the decoupling of chemistry from circuitry, performed once, on one system, and never generalized.

It has not been extended to the sympathetic system, whose very name encodes the conflation, and the phenomena that would have forced it -play, recruiting that system's architecture without its characteristic chemistry; intimacy, recruiting dorsal vagal architecture under safety -were absorbed as hybrid states, co-recruitment of two systems rather than one system under two chemistries.

That the observation was never generalized follows from the form of the neurochemical model the theory inherits, which retains the two-term structure that its own three-term account of neurology was built to supersede.

This is the two-pole constraint: a model with two poles has one axis, so every state it represents must be placed as distance along that line, and shutdown falls at the far end of vigilance rather than outside the line altogether.
The chemistry that would place it outside -the endogenous opioids -has no position in such a model, and does not appear in it.

The paper proposes a revised physiological model of the living autonomic nervous system that distinguishes neural circuitry from the neurochemical conditions under which that circuitry operates, together with a specific neurochemical mechanism for the cardiac and respiratory signature of life-threat immobilization, offered as a falsifiable hypothesis and severable from the variable claim it illustrates.
Independently of that distinction, the paper establishes the supradiaphragmatic/subdiaphragmatic partition of the vagus on direct human measurement rather than on comparative inference.
Electron microscopy of human vagal tissue locates a discontinuity at the diaphragm confined to the myelinated population, with large-calibre fiber present above it and absent below.

What the boundary marks is conduction architecture and informational resolution rather than system identity: above the diaphragm temporally precise and spatially specific afferent signalling is available, and below it only the integrated and dispersed.
Because the partition is measured rather than inferred, it holds whether or not the formulation built upon it does.
Consequences follow for the evolutionary framing both parties share.

Of the three functions phylogenetically ordered dissolution performs in the Polyvagal Theory, the present account substitutes for two -escapability rather than phylogenetic age selects the state, and pathology is patterned by the chemistry coupled with recruited neurology, rather than by reversion along a developmental sequence -and refutes the third, since a state enterable without antecedent mobilization is not reached by sequential traversal.
The paper takes no position on whether the phylogenetic account holds.
What it establishes is that the clinical claims do not require it, and that the burden of proof for clinical utility therefore need not rest on a reconstruction that cannot be settled.

Within this framework, observations emphasized by both Porges and Grossman can be understood as accurate relative to the parameters of their descriptions, even though seemingly contradictory, because they are describing different (yet presently unspecified) physiological conditions rather than mutually exclusive conclusions.
The model generates new physiological predictions that can be tested experimentally and offers a pathway for resolving a controversy that has remained intractable for two decades.
The distinctions developed here, and the model that follows from it, arise from Autonomics, a framework of autonomic state set out by the authors in a series of foundation papers. 1

text.text: Polyvagal Theory has become one of the most influential physiological frameworks in traumainformed psychotherapy.
Recent critiques of its neurophysiological foundations have left many clinicians wondering whether the theory should be abandoned, defended, or revised.
The consequences of this dispute extend well beyond the pages of the journals in which it has been conducted.
Over the past two decades it has shaped the training of hundreds of thousands of clinicians and, through them, the care of countless patients and clients.
The recent exchange between Grossman and Porges has therefore left many practitioners in an uncertain position.
If the theory has been fundamentally discredited, should it be abandoned?
If it remains substantially valid, what, if anything, requires revision?
These are not merely academic questions because they bear directly on how clinicians understand safety, threat, connection, and recovery in the people they serve.
For nearly two decades, the debate has stood at an impasse.

Grossman argues that PVT's proposed mechanism is inconsistent with current physiology and evolutionary inference, while Porges argues that the critique does not accurately engage the theory as articulated in the research literature.

Despite repeated exchanges, neither position has produced a framework capable of experimentally resolving the disagreement over the physiology of shutdown. 2, 3, 4 The authors of this paper have applied Polyvagal Theory clinically for decades across trauma treatment, somatic practice, clinical neurology, and psychotherapy.

text.text: They regard it as a framework of considerable clinical value, while also recognizing important gaps in its physiological explanation.

This paper argues that the long-standing dispute between Polyvagal Theory and its critics persists because neither position has built a category for the variable that would adjudicate it: neurochemical context.
The paper traces this distinction in part to the methodological history of neuroanatomy, where neurochemistry and neurology have remained conflated.

That the category was never built follows from the form of the neurochemical model the theory inherits, which retains a two-term structure that Polyvagal Theory's own three-term account of neurology was built to supersede.

By distinguishing neural circuitry from the pervading neurochemistry in which that circuitry operates, the paper proposes a three-variable model of autonomic state (neuroception/ recruited neurology/ pervading neurochemistry) that reconciles key observations emphasized by both sides, generates new and falsifiable physiological predictions, and reframes a two-decade controversy as a question that can, in principle, be tested directly in living human subjects for the first time.
The mechanism proposed is offered as a falsifiable hypothesis; the variable claim does not depend on it.

Porges published The Polyvagal Theory: Neurophysiological Foundations of Emotions, Attachment, Communication, and Self-Regulation in 2011, consolidating research developed since the theory's formulation in 1994.
Clinical uptake was rapid: by the mid-2010s, Deborah Dana and others were translating the theory for clinical and lay audiences.

Dana's work popularized the image of an Autonomic Ladder, with ventral vagal at the top and dorsal vagal at the bottom. 5 In 2020, Porges and colleagues founded the Polyvagal Institute to steward the theory's dissemi-nation.

text.text: In order to address the complexity of the clinician's dilemma, it is useful to distinguish four layers of articulation that seek to describe Polyvagal Theory as it now exists in the world.

With regard to scientific rigor we identify the research layer of evidence derived from physiological research; the clinical layer of evidence derived from direct practice (represented by the Polyvagal Institute's teaching curricula); the meme layer represented in social media and popular culture; and the applied layer 6 as used in commercially licensed technologies such as those developed with the Canadian neuro-technology firm Unyte (including the listening therapies -Safe and Sound Protocol, Rest and Restore Protocol).

text.text: These layers are rarely distinguished by the theory's critics, its popularizers, and even its defenders.

We assert that confusion about the relative truth value of different layers has stalled productive discussion that could otherwise move both research and understanding about clinical intervention with trauma and illness forward.

Grossman's critique, whatever its merits at the research layer, is frequently read by clinical and lay audiences as a thoroughgoing critique ("debunking") of all aspects of the Polyvagal theory, which has provided valuable guidance in clinical circumstances, as evidenced by clinically significant empirical results.

Yet Porges' clarifications about how the critique misses still do not provide adequate guidance for clinicians about the broader implications for practice, or indeed how to counter claims of 'debunking' except in the most esoteric terms.

While this discourse fragmentation partly explains why the exchange has been able to run for twenty years without resolution, it does not by itself explain why the exchange has been unresolvable even at the research layer, where both Grossman and Porges are arguing in good faith from their own research and the primary literature.

That deeper reason is that while both parties have been well-equipped to argue about anatomy and evolution, neither has systematically applied, in the conceptual vocabulary of autonomic state construction, a category for the variable that would actually adjudicate their central empirical disagreement about the physiology -which is the argument developed in Section 4, after the necessary groundwork of Section 3, and formalized in Section 5.
The methodological concerns considered in this section predate Polyvagal Theory, yet describe the neuro-taxonomy that both Porges and Grossman inherited and are working from.
They are relevant to the present dispute for a specific reason.
The anatomical maps inherited by contemporary autonomic neuroscience were necessarily constructed under methodological constraints, including the study of postmortem tissue.

Those constraints matter here insofar as they encourage fixed functional identities to be assigned to neural structures whose physiological expression in a living organism is context dependent, including depending on variable neurochemical context.
The argument that follows invites revision of established neuroanatomy while concurrently asking whether anatomy alone is sufficient to explain autonomic function.

A category error occurs when a claim properly belonging to one logical category is treated as though it belonged to another. 7 The construction of the foundational maps of neuroanatomy has been shaped by a sequence of distinct, self-reinforcing category errors: the conflation of correlation with identity, the conflation of distinct levels of description, the conflation of tissue preservation with in vivo presentation, the conflation of visual differentiability with neurophysiological distinctness, and the granting of causal centrality to structures whose apparent primacy reflects a discipline that has historically located explanatory authority in cognition, rather than any demonstrated primacy in the regulation of autonomic state.

text.text: Each error compounds the last: a taxonomy built on one mistaken category becomes the substrate on which the next category error is constructed, until the resulting neural cartography reflects the sequence of methods by which the nervous system was studied more than the organization of the nervous system itself.
The central category error this paper diagnoses did not originate with Porges, and it is not a defect of Polyvagal Theory specifically.

It is inherited broadly by the discipline of autonomic science from the methodological conditions under which modern neuroanatomy constructed its foundational maps, as detailed at length in Forest Not Lumberyard: Methodological Bias, Structural Error, and a Necessary Transformation of the Epistemic Ground of Autonomic Neuroanatomy. 1 Four compounding conditions are relevant here.
text.formatted: It is inherited broadly by the discipline of autonomic science from the methodological conditions under which modern neuroanatomy constructed its foundational maps, as detailed at length in Forest Not Lumberyard: Methodological Bias, Structural Error, and a Necessary Transformation of the Epistemic Ground of Autonomic Neuroanatomy. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">1</ref> Four compounding conditions are relevant here.

text.text: Three are summarized here (arguments 1,2, and 4 from that paper) while developed at length there ; the third (argument 3) is elaborated below, because its argument is load-bearing for this paper.
The first is the methodological hegemony of necrotic anatomy: cadaver dissection as the epistemic standard for the originating neuro-anatomical maps in the field.

Post mortem study conserves large-diameter myelinated fiber, yet the finest fibers in the nervous system are a hundredth the width of a human hair, and the fine-fiber network through which the living autonomic nervous system receives the majority of its afferent input degrades before it can be observed. 8, 9 The received maps are therefore devoid of the fine fiber that is their instantiation in living tissue: they are maps of autonomic trunkline structure rather than maps of autonomic structure.

text.text: If the living ANS is an Oak tree in summer, the inherited maps represent winter-bare Oaks.

The second is the hegemony of visuality: visual differentiation of gross structure in the cadaver was established as the epistemic standard, reifying structural artifacts as neurophysiological fact, so that nomenclature separates structures which are physiologically and functionally contiguous -the brainstem from the spinal cord -across a transition that distributed autonomic and sensorimotor circuits span continuously.

The fourth is the brain-centric bias, and it is tiered: modern neuroscience is cognition-centric: it grants causal centrality to structures whose apparent primacy reflects a discipline that has historically located explanatory authority in cognition (central-over-peripheral bias).

In addition, the autonomic nervous system is roughly 80 percent afferent and the peripheral ANS primarily extra-cranial 10 , yet models of autonomic organization have generally been built around central structures and their motor efferent outputs, partly because differentiating afferent autonomic from somatic fibers has been challenging (output-over-input bias).

text.text: Langley, who introduced the term 'autonomic' in 1898, defined the system by its efferent pathways, restricting the category to visceral motor fibers and placing afferents outside it. 11 The restriction was definitional rather than provisional: afferents were not omitted pending better methods, they were put beyond the boundary of the category.

text.text: The boundary has not since been redrawn.

What it produces is a nomenclature in which every term names an output, applied to a system four fifths of which (between 73.9% and 80+%) is input -a convention that inverts what the autonomic nervous system is: a refined surveillance intelligence, named for the motor outputs by which it modulates organs, glands and the vasculature.

An interoceptive listening and modulation system named only for its modulation componentry: its primary afferent intelligence undifferentiated and except in cases where it is resolved through electron microscopy, largely invisible.
Polyvagal Theory inherits and continues aspects of both biases.

Every structural term in the framework names an efferent structure or an efferent pathway: the ventral vagal complex and its nucleus ambiguus, the dorsal vagal complex and its dorsal motor nucleus, the myelinated cardiac efferents, the special visceral efferents of the trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, the social engagement system, the face-heart connection, the vagal brake.

On the afferent side the framework names only termination sites -the nucleus of the solitary tract and, for the ventral vagal complex, the source nuclei of the facial and trigeminal nervesand gives the afferent fibers themselves no structural terms and no partitions.
The asymmetry is not an interpretation of the theory; it is a list of its terms.

Neuroception, which the theory makes causally prior to all of them (the moment to moment neural detection of safety, danger, or lifethreat), spans every afferent receptor in the body, every fiber that carries their signal inward, and whatever structures integrate them -and is specified at none of those levels.
The most consequential revision to autonomic science in fifty years specifies almost none of what the autonomic nervous system is made of.

It also inherits unquestioned the close conceptual association between sympathetic neurology and its characteristic neurochemistry and, in the parasympathetic direction, closely associates the dorsal vagal complex with immobilization.
Comparatively less attention has been given to how differing neurochemical environments might alter the functional expression of the same circuitry.
The third of these four category errors is the conflation of neurochemistry with neurology, a category already two centuries old when the chemistry arrived to be absorbed into it.

In 1904, T. R. Elliott observed that administration of epinephrine (a catecholamine) produced physiological effects resembling sympathetic nervous system activation. 12 The observation was foundational in bridging neurology to neurochemistry.

text.text: This led to Dale in 1914 characterizing acetylcholine's actions and distinguishing muscarinic from nicotinic effects, noting the resemblance to parasympathetic stimulation, then Loewi's subsequent identification of Vagusstoff (1921), laying groundwork for Loewi and Dale's 1936 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, awarded for discoveries relating to chemical transmission of nerve impulses.

Over time, the close association between sympathetic activation and catecholamine release reified a conceptual model where the anatomical system and its characteristic neurochemical milieu are treated as a single functional entity, e.g., the Sympathetic Nervous System.

While the identification of a specific neurotransmitter with a specific pathway proves almost tautological -without noradrenaline at the sympathetic neuroeffector junction there is no sympathetic signal -the categorical claim is something else: that sympathetic names a chemicallydefined identity.

That claim was so entrenched that it went unexamined even when von Euler demonstrated, in 1946, that Elliott had named the wrong catecholamine. 13 The sympathetic transmitter is not epinephrine, as Elliott had proposed: it is norepinephrine.

text.text: The correction is more instructive than its reception suggests.

Elliott's evidence was an administered substance reproducing a system's functional signature, and the inference drawn from it was identity between that substance and the neurology (e.g., epinephrine is the sympathetic neurotransmitter).

Forty-two years later the substance in the inference proved not to be the system's transmitter at all -yet the identity survived, one catecholamine (norepinephrine) substituted for another (epinephrine), its form untouched by the replacement of its content.
A claim indifferent to which molecule satisfies it is not a claim about a molecule.
It is a claim about where the identity of a system resides.
What the field had taken for a finding about physiology was functioning as a convention of classification.
The finding carried a further implication that went undrawn.
How could a substance that is not the sympathetic transmitter produce that system's characteristic effects?
Only because those effects are determined at the receptor rather than at the nerve.

Epinephrine acts at the same adrenoceptors on target tissues through which postganglionic sympathetic fibers signal, and a receptor is indifferent to how its ligand -any molecule that binds it -arrived.
Neurotransmission is one means of delivering a ligand to a receptor but it is not what produces the effect.
A substance that is not a system's transmitter had therefore been reproducing that system's output for four decades, which establishes that the output was never diagnostic of the pathway.
Chemistry and neurology were demonstrably separable in 1946.
The demonstration was read as a correction to which molecule holds the title.

It was in fact a demonstration that the title had never been the kind of thing a molecule could hold -that what Elliott's experiment could es-tablish, pharmacological sufficiency at a receptor, and what the field took it to have established, the chemical identity of a neural system, were never the same claim.
Epinephrine's own position in the sympathetic system illustrates why a two-term account of that system's chemistry was never sufficient.

Endogenously, epinephrine is not a junctional transmitter but a circulating hormone released from the adrenal medulla along the Sympathetic-Adreno-Medullary axis, reaching the same receptors from the bloodstream rather than across a synaptic cleft, and on a timescale of minutes rather than milliseconds.

The consequence is clinically familiar: a defensive mobilization resolves on the timescale of its slowest chemical arm rather than its fastest, which is why activation outlasts the event that provoked it by an interval no account of synaptic transmission would predict.
The characteristic chemistry of the Sympathetic Nervous System has thus comprised more than one mode of action from the beginning.
A third mode is the one this paper takes as its variable, and the three are distinguished by how they act rather than by where they originate.
Neurotransmitters are released at the junction, act within milliseconds, are cleared within milliseconds, and are constitutive of transmission itself.
Neurohormones are released into circulation and reach their receptors at a distance.

Neuromodulators -among them the endogenous opioids, oxytocin, and corticotropin-releasing hormone -are released from varicosities and dendrites as well as from terminals, diffuse beyond the synapse, act over seconds to hours, and signal through receptors that alter the gain of transmission rather than effect it.
They do not carry the signal.
They determine what the signal, once carried, produces: not only the magnitude of a response but its character.

These are modes of action rather than classes of molecule, and the same peptide may act in more than one: oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary into circulation acts as a neurohormone, while oxytocin released centrally from dendrites and varicosities acts as a neuromodulator.

What the present argument requires is therefore a distinction not between substances but between the ways a substance acts upon a circuit -not between molecules, but between the modes in which they behave.
This is what pervading neurochemistry names.
What differs under different modulatory chemistry is not only the magnitude of a response but its kind.
The same circuitry, differently suffused, yields states that diverge in affective character and valence rather than in intensity alone.

On the account developed here, the modulatory environment is therefore a determinant of what a state is rather than only of how strongly it is expressed -which is why shutdown is not a more extreme mobilization, and is not experienced as one.
This third category -how the chemicals act -was unavailable when the taxonomy was fixed.

Volume transmission, peptide co-release, and receptor-level modulation of synaptic gain entered the literature well after the nomenclature had settled; the enkephalins were not isolated until 1975. 14 The vocabulary in which the autonomic systems were named was transmitter vocabulary, because transmitter chemistry was the only chemistry the field had available at the time.

text.text: A taxonomy assembled from one class of molecule will not readily accommodate a second class whose defining property is that it alters what the first class accomplishes.

The identification of a specific neurochemistry with a specific pathway therefore obscures a distinction the field had no means of drawing at the time the identification was made: the same neural architecture may participate in markedly different physiological states depending upon the neuromodulatory environment in which it operates.
A similar pattern is reproduced in later interpretations of parasympathetic function, including the dorsal vagal system described in Polyvagal Theory.
Anatomical pathways are assigned stable functional identities on the basis of the neurochemical conditions under which they are most commonly observed.
Yet that stability does not hold when those conditions change.
This is why pervading neurochemistry constitutes a third variable rather than a re-description of the second.
Transmitter chemistry is not separable from recruited neurology: it is what recruitment consists of, and a model naming both would be counting one thing twice.

Modulatory chemistry is separable -the same circuit, intact and equally recruited, produces different physiological output as its modulatory environment changes -and the degree of that separability is the explanatory space the three-variable model occupies.
The distinction is the difference between a model in which anatomy predicts function and a model in which anatomy predicts only what is available to be modulated.
The distinction applies directly to the system this conflation names.

The spinal vertebrate architecture conventionally designated sympathetic is one of the neurological systems governing autonomic regulation of viscera, glands and the vascular system, and it houses central pattern generators for hard-wired biobehavioral patterns -including complex patterned movement, visceral regulation, and various autonomic reflexes -in brainstem nuclei and in dorsal horn and sympathetic ganglia chain structures.

The pervading neurochemistry that suffuses this architecture when the body detects danger is a separate matter: the circulating catecholamines of the Sympathetic-Adreno-Medullary axis; the glucocorticoids of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal axis; and whatever modulatory peptides the context recruits.
Naming the architecture and the chemistry with a single term makes the second of them invisible.
The same neurology is regularly recruited outside threat.
It is recruited in play.
It is recruited whenever centrally pattern-generated movement is required, including hard-wired autonomic reflexes.

The neurology comprising the Sympathetic Nervous System has life-sustaining functions that have nothing to do with fight-or-flight, and a nomenclature naming it for one chemical context obscures every other context in which it operates.
Yet this conflation should not come as a surprise.

The Roman physician Galen of Pergamon named the concept of sympathy between parts, illustrating it by dissecting pigs and monkeys and extrapolating his findings to human anatomy; the notion was later taken up in the term Sympathetic Nervous System.
By 1732 Winslow had popularized the great sympathetic nerve.

By the time chemical neurotransmission was established as a systematic principle of the nervous system, with the Nobel Prize to Loewi and Dale in 1936, the reification of the Sympathetic Nervous System as a single entity had stood for two hundred years.
The chemistry did not found the category.
It arrived to a category already built, and was absorbed into it.

The present model holds instead that many autonomic circuits are context-dependent, their functional expression emerging from the interaction of neural architecture, neuroception, and pervading neurochemistry rather than from anatomy alone.
The critical question is therefore not which circuit is active, but how the same circuit behaves under different neuroceptive and neurochemical conditions.
Neither party to the present dispute has asked this question.
Porges accounts for dorsal vagal shutdown without naming the neuromodulators that would be active in a life-threat response.

Grossman tests the prediction that dorsal vagal states produce bradycardia against a clinical literature of emotional freezing and dissociation, accepting Polyvagal Theory's assignment of those states to the dorsal vagal complex -when the assignment is what required examination.
What these four inherited errors have in common is that each converts a limitation of method into a feature of the object.

The received taxonomy of the autonomic nervous system is a record of what could be seen in dead tissue, named in the vocabulary available at the time of naming, and it has been read ever since as a description of how the living system is organized.
Of the four, it is the conflation of neurochemistry with neurology that bears most directly on the dispute this paper addresses.
Neural circuitry supplies the architecture through which autonomic regulation occurs.
It does not, by itself, determine what that regulation produces.
Seemingly incompatible assertions by Porges and Grossman et al. may both be true if the appropriate neurochemical context is factored in.

The Autonomics model proposes that engagement of subdiaphragmatic vagal architecture (the Porgesian dorsal vagal system) in the absence of endogenous opioid activity is not by itself sufficient to produce either the profound bradycardia or the respiratory suppression that characterize the state.
Instead, we propose that this circuitry participates in ordinary visceral regulation as well as defensive states.

Therefore, when Grossman asserts that there is no consistent correlation between activation of this circuit and bradycardia, he is provisionally accurate. 4 The Grossman et al. critique of Polyvagal Theory levels six specific charges: (1) that Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia is not a direct and reliable measure of central vagal outflow to the heart; (2) that PVT's characterizations of the neuroanatomy and function of the Nucleus Ambiguus and Dorsal Motor Nucleus are inaccurate; (3) that PVT's account of vagal evolution is inaccurate; (4) that PVT's characterization of mammalian social behavior relative to non-mammalian vertebrates is inaccurate; (5) that PVT misinterprets earlier seminal physiological literature; and (6) that its core psychological tenets predate the theory's own elaboration.

The central load-bearing neurophysiological argument the Grossman et al. paper uses to critique PVT is that in clinical contexts, ordinary human emotional freezing and dissociation do not necessarily produce the massive, sudden heart-rate deceleration that Polyvagal Theory's universalizing account of "dorsal vagal shutdown" predicts.

The literature Grossman cites on this point is not in dispute. 15 Nor is the RSA critique, that other signals may be more comprehensive registers of vagal tone -a concession made here without reservation, and one that becomes load-bearing in Section 8, where the same methodological argument is turned on the states the dispute is attempting to distinguish.

text.text: Grossman correctly emphasizes that RSA is influenced by multiple interacting physiological variables, complicating its interpretation as a direct index of vagal tone or global autonomic state.
Yet neither of these concessions resolves the controversy, because neither touches the actual point of failure.
The point of failure is structural, and is shared by both parties.
Both frameworks place primary explanatory weight on neural circuitry.

Porges says that life-threat is mediated by a subdiaphragmatic vagal circuit with origins in the Dorsal Motor Nucleus 17 while Grossman argues that activation of this complex doesn't reliably produce bradycardia. 15 Yet these seemingly contradictory accounts may both be true if differentiating neurochemical context is factored in.

text.text: It would be inaccurate to characterize Polyvagal Theory as lacking a neurochemical dimension.

In April 2026, Porges co-authored a comprehensive review of neuropeptide regulation of the brain-heart axis, and the review demonstrates that the theory has acquired a developed neurochemical vocabulary. 18 What that vocabulary is used for is the assignment to each system of its characteristic molecule: oxytocin to vagal modulation and social buffering, vasopressin to social vigilance and sympathetic activation, corticotropin-releasing hormone to stress reactivity, the urocortins to recovery.

text.text: This is the identification of a system with its chemistry, performed at the level of the peptide and with a larger cast than the catecholamine formulation it extends.
The review does state a principle of context-dependence, and what that principle governs is worth stating precisely.

Identical stressors may be adaptive in one physiological context and maladaptive in another, and the determinant named is the organism's baseline autonomic organization -specifically, the accessibility of ventral vagal cardioinhibitory regulation. 18 That is a claim about which system is available to respond, not about what a given system produces under a given chemistry.

text.text: Anatomy continues to determine function; context determines only which anatomy the organism begins from.
The genuine decoupling appears once in the Polyvagal literature, in the founding formulation.

The 2001 paper pairs an oxytocin-conditioned account of calm immobilization with a vasopressin-conditioned account of immobilized fear, at identical dorsal vagal anatomy. 17 One circuit, two chemistries, two states differing in kind.

text.text: The observation was never raised to a principle, 19 never extended to the sympathetic system whose name encodes the conflation most directly, and the phenomena that would have forced the extension -play, which recruits sympathetic architecture without fight-or-flight chemistry, and intimacy, which recruits dorsal vagal architecture under safety -were absorbed instead as hybrid states, co-recruitment of two systems rather than one system under two chemistries.

text.text: The theory therefore performed the decoupling without generalizing it, and has not turned it on the system where the dispute is located.
Why the observation was not generalized is a question the shape of the neurochemical model answers.

Polyvagal Theory's founding achievement was the replacement of a two-term neurological model -the paired antagonism of sympathetic and parasympathetic, expressed clinically as autonomic balance -with a three-term one.
That move is the theory's most durable contribution, and the Autonomics framework retains it.
The neurochemical model has not made the corresponding move.

The 2026 review treats four neuropeptides, and they resolve into two poles: oxytocin and the urocortins supporting social buffering and autonomic flexibility, vasopressin and corticotropin-releasing hormone promoting vigilance and allostatic effort.
Dysregulation is defined as a shift of that balance toward one pole.

The term the review uses for the relation is balance, which appears fifty-six times in its body text. 20 Two further peptides have been added to the 2017 oxytocin-vasopressin formulation without a third position being added to the model.

text.text: The binary resides in the architecture, not in the number of molecules.
No claim of descent is made here.
The oxytocin-vasopressin opposition arose independently, in comparative neuroendocrinology, and owes nothing genealogically to Langley and Cannon.

The observation is one of form rather than lineage: the neurochemical model Polyvagal Theory articulates reproduces the same two-term antagonistic structure that the neurological model was constructed to supersede.

Paired antagonism is the least expensive structure available for representing a regulatory system, and it recurs for that reason -the same structural attractor that, in the anatomical domain, produced the reified trunk-line maps this paper's companion work addresses.
This also accounts for the fate of the 2001 observation.

The decoupling performed there was conducted within the two-pole chemistry -oxytocin against vasopressin -and those two poles are exactly what it found: a dorsal vagal state under affiliative chemistry, and a dorsal vagal state under vigilance chemistry.
The second is what Polyvagal Theory has named 'dorsal vagal shutdown' ever since, and what the 2001 paper itself calls 'immobilized fear'.
Vasopressin was the terminal position the chemistry afforded, and that is where the life-threat state was placed.
Reaching the state the clinical record describes would have required a third chemistry, and the model had no position for one.
The binary did not obstruct the decoupling.
It bounded what the decoupling could find.
A model with two poles has one axis.
Increasing threat can be represented only as distance along it -the two-pole constraint -and shutdown must therefore be located at the far end of the vigilance pole.

That is where the 2001 formulation placed it, at the point where fight-orflight behaviours were no longer an option; and it is where the 2026 review places it still: past the risk zone, under allostatic overload, with the dorsal vagal complex predominating at high challenge intensity. 18 Twenty-five years and a developed neurochemical vocabulary separate the two statements, and the position is unchanged -because the position follows from the shape of the model rather than from its contents.

text.text: This renders shutdown a quantitative extreme of mobilization rather than a state categorically distinct from it.
It is the autonomic ladder's error, reappearing at the level of chemistry: more threat, further along a single line.
And it is the specific proposition the clinical record contra-dicts.

Shutdown correlates with lowered heart rate rather than elevated, with numbness and interoceptive deficit rather than heightened visceral distress, with immobilization rather than mobilization, with dissociation rather than fear or rage.
It is not more of the same.
It is different in kind, and a neurochemical model with an affiliation pole and a vigilance pole has nowhere to put it.
That inability is not new.
It is the one the two-term neurological model had, and the one the second vagus was introduced to resolve.
What the chemistry has reproduced is not only the structure Polyvagal Theory superseded, but the particular failure that made superseding it necessary.

In the 2026 review -a comprehensive treatment of neuropeptide regulation of the brain-heart axis under stress and threat, running to some three hundred references -the endogenous opioid system appears once, as a mediator of ischemic preconditioning, in a passage unrelated to defense.
The terms enkephalin, endorphin, dynorphin, naltrexone and naloxone do not appear at all, and neither does dissociation. 21 Two things make the omission specific.

text.text: The review's stated scope is four evolutionarily conserved neuropeptides, and the opioid peptides are evolutionarily conserved neuropeptides; the criterion admits them.

The topic falls within scope by the review's own account, since it proposes that dorsal vagal pathways may mediate immobilization responses under extreme threat and places shutdown on its central figure.
The opioid peptides are also the one family for which a human clinical literature on immobilization already exists.
Antagonists have been tested against dissociative and immobilization phenomena in human patients for three decades.

An open-label trial reports naltrexone reducing dissociation, analgesia and tonic immobility together, and a systematic review of the comparative literature reports a pooled effect favouring opioid antagonists, with high heterogeneity and possible publication bias. 22 A review of neuropeptide regulation of the brain-heart axis under threat is the natural place for that literature to be weighed.

text.text: The 2026 review passes over it, and the reason is structural rather than evidential: the questions a model can pose are bounded by the positions it contains, and a two-pole chemistry contains two.

Polyvagal Theory identified the circuitry: a subdiaphragmatic vagal pathway, distinct in origin and myelination from the pathway governing social engagement, recruited under life-threat and capable of profound cardioinhibition.

Grossman et al. established that the circuitry is not sufficient, since across the clinical literature on human emotional freezing and dissociation its engagement is not reliably accompanied by that bradycardia. 4 Both findings are sound.

text.text: The dispute has been unresolvable because each party describes one term of a product.
In the absence of endogenous opioids, dorsal vagal shutdown neurology is not sufficient to induce bradycardia.
The state requires the conjunction: subdiaphragmatic vagal engagement under neuroception of life-threat, within a pervading endogenous opioid chemistry.
Porges measured the circuit and found the state; Grossman measured the circuit and did not.
Neither specified the chemistry, so neither result could discriminate.
That inescapable stress recruits endogenous opioid activity in humans is established by antagonism rather than assay.

Veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder viewing combat footage showed a thirty per cent reduction in pain intensity under placebo and none under naloxone, with that change discriminating the groups more strongly than any other variable measured; peripheral peptide and hormone assays showed nothing, and the authors concluded central mediation. 23 The placement of that chemistry is also established.

text.text: The defense cascade model derived from the animal literature assigns unresponsive immobility -parasympathetic dominance, depersonalization and derealization -to the ventrolateral periaqueductal column, and assigns the kappa and mu opioids to that phase, implicating them in immobility and in downregulation of the sympathetic nervous system. 24 The same model names the cardiorespiratory profile of the state as immobilization, bradycardia and apnoea, and attributes it to the dorsal vagal complex. 24 Both terms occupy the same phase of the same model, and the model does not join them.

text.text: The present account joins them.

The claim is correspondingly narrow: it specifies that the state is a product of two terms rather than a function of either, and that the second term has gone unspecified while the first was adjudicated.
The cardiorespiratory signature of the conjoined state has never been measured against opioid activity in a living human being.
This synthesis now provides a predictive matrix whereby the standing twenty-year controversy between Porges and Grossman can be adjudicated in living human subjects for the first time.

A central source of confusion in the Porges/Grossman controversy is that the key terminology that Grossman and Porges are respectively using to denote the autonomic states and subjective expereinces under consideration do not align terminologically.

The states under consideration map the defense cascade in its transition from active defense, through tonic immobility, through shutdown and collapse, but Porges and Grossman's terminology talk past one another.
Grossman uses the convention of a term called 'emotional freezing', which might seem to align with Porges use of the term freezing, but does not.
When Porges is talking about 'freezing', he is referring to tonic immobility.
These terms occupy different locations on the defense cascade.
In order to adjudicate the claims on an apples-to-apples basis, we have to align terminology Figure 3.

text.text: Tonic Immobility refers to an autonomic state where the body is rigid and muscle tone remains high, and the heart shows a deceleration dominated by parasympathetic drive rather than the profound bradycardia that characterizes shutdown. 25 This state is accompanied by concurrent sympathetic and parasympathetic upregulation.

text.text: The respiratory signature of tonic immobility is a matter of record rather than inference, and it is not what the term suggests.
Tonic immobility is bradypnoeic and regularized, not apnoeic.

Plethysmography in the mouse finds that where active exploration produces irregular breathing between three and twelve hertz, tonic immobility drops the frequency into a narrow band near four hertz while the variability of both frequency and tidal volume collapses. 27 Thermocouple recording with simultaneous olfactory bulb local field potentials finds the same: during tonic immobility respiration becomes steady with little cycle-to-cycle variability. 28 The two laboratories differ on the causal role of olfactory input and agree on the pattern.

text.text: The distinguishing feature is regularity rather than rate.
Breathing in tonic immobility is metronomic; shutdown breathing is absent.
The absolute frequencies are in a mouse model and do not transfer: the pattern does.
The regularization has a mechanism, and on the account given here it is the same chemistry.

The variability of the breathing rhythm derives from the many weak inputs that can carry the generating network to its bursting threshold -what Feldman terms the lability of the rhythm. 29 Opioid action slows the emergent process by which that network assembles toward synchrony, and raises dose-dependently the threshold at which an input triggers a burst.

text.text: Under moderate opioid load the phasic inputs that ordinarily vary breathing from breath to breath no longer reach that threshold while a tonic mobilizing drive still does.
What survives is a rhythm driven by a single steady input: narrow in frequency, uniform in volume, and clinically forced.
Under heavier load the tonic drive also fails, and the rhythm stops.
This is the structure the cardiac account already describes.
In tonic immobility the heart is sustained humorally while neural cardioacceleratory drive is suppressed; the breath is sustained by tonic drive while phasic modulation is suppressed.
What the blockade removes in both cases is the modulated component.
Tonic immobility is not partial shutdown.

It is the selective loss of the variable component of two outputs, and a single parameter -the threshold at which an input produces an output -orders all three states: many inputs reaching threshold in the ordinary case, one in tonic immobility, none in shutdown.
Shutdown is characterized by loss of muscle tone, profound physiological slowing, analgesia, and -on the clinical observation reported here -apnea. 30 No vagal account of the state predicts all four.
text.formatted: Shutdown is characterized by loss of muscle tone, profound physiological slowing, analgesia, and -on the clinical observation reported here -apnea. <ref type="bibr">30</ref> No vagal account of the state predicts all four.

text.text: One feature of the respiratory component distinguishes a failure of drive from an obstruction of its expression, and it is clinically legible.
Where air hunger is present, inspiratory drive is being generated and its expression is being opposed.
Where air hunger is absent, drive is not being generated -which accounts for the clinical observation that the deepest presentations are not experienced as suffocation.
Air hunger is read from the physiology rather than reported, its presence appearing as struggle and its absence as indifference.

The authors' clinical observation is that this distinction governs which interventions the state will accept. 30 Clinical observation across two decades of practice indicates that shutdown is entered by two routes, and that the distinction between them is not visible in the state itself.

text.text: In the first, threat converts from escapable to inescapable while active defense is already in progress: escape is inhibited, the state shifts into tonic immobility with muscle tone high and catecholamines circulating, and collapse follows as the circulating pool clears.
In the second, shutdown is the default defensive configuration, and a minor or objectively trivial threat produces it directly.

There may be a brief catecholamine registration, but active defense is not an available pathway -the system is conditioned to bypass it, 31 typically from an early period in which expressing active defense produced worse outcomes.

text.text: No mobilization is suppressed, because none was mounted.

The epistemic status of this distinction is clinical observation: it is strong evidence for the existence of the two presentations and for the discrimination being one an observer reliably makes, and it is not evidence for their prevalence.
The consequence is a prediction about recovery rather than about state, and it is the sharper of the two.
Recovery from shutdown entered through mobilization requires a context capable of discharging that mobilization, and the person returns through the rage or terror that was suppressed.
Recovery from shutdown entered directly reveals no such mobilization, because none was suppressed, and the state can reorganize into connection without passing through activation at all.
The mobilization is physiological; its discharge is physiological.
Describing a mobilization is not the same act as moving it, and a verbal account of one, while evoking its physiological salience, does not constitute its discharge.
Where no context adequate to that physiological discharge is available, the arousal released by resolution has nowhere to go, and the state does not return to baseline.
What must occur occurs in the body.
It does not occur in language, even though language can evoke its salience.

The phenomenology clinicians record in shutdown converges on the phenomenology of opioid administration: a surreal or dreamlike quality, uncertainty as to whether one is awake, a sensation of floating, and -most specifically -analgesia. 30 The last of these is the one that discriminates.

text.text: Derealization has many causes.
Analgesia has few, and none of them is anatomical: no property of a vagal pathway, dorsal or ventral, predicts that a person sustaining injury will not feel it.

Stress-induced analgesia is a well-characterized phenomenon with both opioid-dependent and opioid-independent forms. 32, 33 An account that locates shutdown in anatomy alone leaves peritraumatic analgesia unexplained.

text.text: An account that locates it in a pervading opioid chemistry predicts it, and predicts which stressors will fail to produce it.
A second feature of the phenomenology discriminates on the same grounds, and is more readily observed than analgesia because it requires no injury.
What patients describe during shutdown is not calm but indifference: the circumstance is registered and does not matter.

That is the affective signature of µ-opioid action, in which the sensory component of an aversive state per-sists while its motivational force is removed, and it is not the signature of parasympathetic quiescence, which presents as ease rather than as detachment.
No efferent vagal pathway predicts motivational indifference, any more than it predicts analgesia.

The distinction also accounts for a feature of the clinical presentation that would otherwise be puzzling: a state that presents subjectively as equanimity is not one people seek help for, and its prevalence is correspondingly underestimated.

By 2020, Porges' model had already introduced tonic immobility as a hybrid state, 37 structurally distinct from the four pure single-system states of which dorsal vagal shutdown is one -this taxonomic separation existed years before Grossman's critique was published.

text.text: What the framework did not supply was the neurochemical specification that would let the distinction perform empirical work.

Absent it, tonic immobility and shutdown remain distinguished by recruited efferent neural circuitry but not by pervading neurochemistry, and the theory does not generate differentiated physiological predictions despite distinguishing the states descriptively within its taxonomy.
Dissociation is something different again.
It describes a person's subjective experience -a sense of disconnection from the body, the environment, or the self.
Dissociation may accompany tonic immobility, shutdown, placating, or other autonomic states, but it is not itself an autonomic state.

This account is testable in a way the current debate is not, because it generates distinct predictions for each state rather than treating anatomy as the sole predictor, and because the variable that discriminates between them can be specified in advance of the experiment.
That variable is escapability, not threat magnitude.
Confirmed neuroception of life-threat under an escapable condition should produce transient and non-opioid analgesia, and leave the heart accelerated.

Confirmed neuroception of life-threat under an inescapable condition should produce long-lasting opioid-dependent analgesia, and the cardiac and respiratory profile described above. 38, 39 The respiratory predictions are the most readily tested and require no pharmacological intervention at all.

text.text: If shutdown is apnoeic and tonic immobility is regularized, the two states are distinguishable at the bedside with a respiratory band 40, 41 -independent of cardiac measurement, and independent of any judgment as to which neural pathway is active.

text.text: The authors' clinical observation is that the distinction holds.
It has not been formally measured yet.
A consequence follows for the measurement literature, and it follows from Grossman's own methodological argument rather than against it.
Grossman's position, which this paper concedes, is that respiratory sinus arrhythmia is confounded by respiratory parameters and cannot be read as a direct index of vagal tone.
The states under dispute are precisely those in which those parameters change systematically: regularized and slowed in tonic immobility, absent in shutdown.

Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in these states is therefore not merely noisy but systematically biased in a state-dependent way -a limitation that is structural in the index itself, which measures the cardiac response to respiratory modulation without measuring the respiratory signal 40 -and the direction of the bias differs between the two states the dispute is attempting to distinguish.

text.text: In an apnoeic state the case is stronger still: there is no respiratory frequency, and the index is not imprecise but undefined.

Protocols that have sought dorsal vagal bradycardia using respiratory sinus arrhythmia as the index of vagal engagement would, in the state this paper describes, be applying a measure that collapses for reasons unrelated to vagal tone.
Each of these predictions is falsifiable in a living subject using measures already available.
Sympathetic tone can be indexed independently of vagal tone, and respiration can be measured directly.
None of them requires resolving what happened in the vagus nerve of a fish four hundred million years ago.

A significant portion of this twenty-year debate -the evolution of vagal control from cardiorespiratory synchrony in fish to RSA in mammals, the phylogenetic status of myelinated versus unmyelinated cardioinhibitory fibers, the recapitulationist logic both PVT and its critics have accused each other of -has been conducted on evolutionary terrain.
Evolutionary claims about vertebrate lineages separated by hundreds of millions of years cannot be tested in a living organism, by either party, under any protocol.
The three-variable model does not settle the debate by being a better theory of vagal evolution.

It settles the specific bradycardia dispute by relocating the question to something that can be directly observed in a living human being in real time -which evolutionary inference, by definition, cannot be.

A second relocation is available on the same ground, and Section 5 makes it: the partition of the vagus at the respiratory diaphragm, which both parties have argued comparatively, can be measured directly in human tissue.
The terrain of the dispute is escapable in two directions -toward what a living subject can be observed to do, and toward what a human nerve can be shown to contain.

Grossman's critique, for all its anatomical detail, does not fully penetrate the problem, because it is conducted on much the same terrain Polyvagal Theory itself is built on: comparative anatomy and evolutionary inference across species.

The critique does not fully penetrate the problem because it is a consequence of asking a question -which nucleus, which fiber type, in which species -that does not reach the level at which the current model proposes the error exists.
The clinical phenomenon Porges set out to explain in 1994 was not new.

A cardioinhibitory, immobilized presentation, distinct from the cardioacceleratory, mobilized presentation of fightor-flight, had been documented clinically since shell-shocked soldiers returned from the First World War.

What Polyvagal Theory contributed was not the observation, which predates it by nearly a century, but a plausible neural mechanism for it: a phylogenetically-ordered dissolution, in which a brainstem structure older in evolutionary terms than the one governing social engagement took over under sufficient threat.
The mechanism was clinically plausible, and it was this plausibility, anchored to a neurological explanation, that carried the theory's rapid ascent through clinical practice.
What the present model offers in its place is not a different pathway but a different kind of explanation.
This distinction changes the scientific question.
Grossman's critique asks which brainstem nuclei or vagal pathways mediate bradycardia, which is an appropriate question if anatomy alone is assumed to determine function.
The present model asks a different question: how does neurochemical context alter the physiological expression of the same neural circuitry?
Because these are different mechanisms, anatomical evidence alone cannot distinguish between them.

The advantage of the present model is threefold: (1) it aligns more closely with clinical observation, (2) it generates predictions that can be tested directly in living human subjects, and (3) it accounts for the immobilized, cardioinhibitory presentation without requiring a phylogenetic explanation.

Of the explanatory work the dissolution account performs, the present account substitutes for two parts: the state is selected by whether escape is available rather than by the evolutionary age of the structure recruited, and patterned degradation follows from the chemistry rather than from reversion along a developmental order.
The third part, a fixed sequence of recruitment, it does not substitute for but contradicts, since a state enterable without antecedent mobilization is not arrived at by traversal.

This paper takes no position on whether the phylogenetic account holds, and the third advantage is that the question need not be settled: the central hypothesis does not depend upon reconstructing the evolutionary history of the vagus nerve, and can be evaluated instead by examining how neural activity and neurochemical state interact to produce autonomic responses in real time in living humans.
The burden of proof for clinical utility is thereby detached from a reconstruction that cannot ever be demonstrated in a living subject.

The untenability verdict does not follow, because neither side has directly tested the condition that the present model identifies as critical: confirmed life-threat accompanied by evidence of endogenous opioid activity.
What breaks the stasis in the Polyvagal controversy is the claim that pervading neurochemistry is a determining variable in whether bradycardia occurs at all.

Were the opioid account proposed here to prove wrong in its particulars, the structure of the disagreement would be unchanged: both parties would still be adjudicating an anatomical question whose answer is conditional on a variable neither has specified, and the protocols that have failed to elicit dorsal vagal bradycardia would still have failed for want of a precondition rather than for want of a pathway.
The mechanism is offered as falsifiable.
The variable is what the paper asks the field to adopt.

This paper does not attempt to resolve the comparative anatomy of the nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus across species, nor adjudicate the evolutionary claims regarding cardiorespiratory coupling from fish to mammals.
It declines those questions because its claims do not require their answers, not because the answers are unavailable: the account advanced here holds whichever way the comparative record is read.
Nor does it contest Grossman's critique of RSA as a vagal tone index, which the authors concede and, in Section 8, extend.

Because the account specifies the chemistry rather than the efferent population, it is indifferent to which vagal nucleus carries the resulting cardioinhibition -and Grossman's correction on that point, that the vagal response to defensive immobilization is mediated primarily by the nucleus ambiguus rather than the dorsal motor nucleus, is accommodated rather than contested here.
Where PVT and its critics disagree on matters outside the neurochemistry/neurology distinction, this paper does not take a position.
The preceding section located a category error at the output end of the model: a neurochemistry conflated with the neurology it accompanies.
A second error of the same structure sits at the input end.
The first can be repaired by enriching the chemistry, while the second reaches the term on which the whole framework rests.
The human vagus is predominantly a sensory nerve.

Immunofluorescent classification of axons in the mid-cervical vagus of eight human body donors finds sensory fibers to constitute 73.9 ± 7.5 per cent of the right nerve and 72.4 ± 5.6 per cent of the left, against 13.2 ± 1.8 and 13.3 ± 3.0 per cent for special visceromotor and parasympathetic fibers combined. 10 Roughly three fibers in four carry information inward.

text.text: Every structural element in that architecture is efferent.
A taxonomy derived from the organization of motor output is thereby applied to a nerve that is three-quarters afferent.

The two structures the framework specifies anatomically account for thirteen per cent of the nerve; the three quarters of it that is sensory maps to the one term the framework does not specify.
This is not an observation that Polyvagal Theory neglects vagal afferents, nor that it inverts the direction of determination.
It does neither.

The nucleus tractus solitarius is present in its architecture, and its causal ordering is explicit and correct: neuroception of safety is the precondition, and engagement of the ventral vagal complex is its consequence.
The difficulty lies at the origin of that sequence rather than in its direction.
Each of the three states is named for the autonomic system that expresses it, while the term that produces them is the one term the theory leaves without a structure.

text.text: What the composition data permit is a direct account of what the inherited anatomical boundary does and does not mark.
Electron microscopy of vagus nerve biopsies procured intra-operatively from organ donors establishes that the discontinuity at the diaphragm is confined to the myelinated population.
The number of unmyelinated fibers does not differ significantly between the cervical and abdominal vagus, at 92,214 ± 17,589 and 79,861 ± 18,210 respectively.

The number of myelinated fibers differs at p = 0.0025, at 19,770 ± 2,851 against 3,000 ± 1,209, as does the ratio of unmyelinated to myelinated fibers. 43 The distributions differ in kind as well as in number: myelinated fiber diameters above the diaphragm fall into two populations, one within the 0-4 µm range and one within the greater-than-four to 9 µm range, while below the diaphragm every myelinated fiber falls within the first. 43 Large-calibre fiber is present above the diaphragm and absent below it.

text.text: The boundary between the supradiaphragmatic and subdiaphragmatic vagus is therefore real, measured directly in human tissue, and independent of any claim about its evolutionary provenance.

Establishing it does not require adjudicating the comparative anatomy of the nucleus ambiguus across vertebrate classes, and it is not disturbed by the finding that myelinated vagal cardiac fibers occur outside the mammals.
This is a point of agreement the present dispute has had no instrument to register: the boundary both parties argue about comparatively can now be measured directly.
What the boundary marks, however, is calibre, and calibre is not the afferent-efferent division.

Given that roughly a third of cervical vagal fibers are myelinated while parasympathetic and special visceromotor fibers together account for thirteen per cent, a substantial myelinated afferent population follows arithmetically. 10 The myelination gradient cuts through the sensory system rather than around it.

text.text: This is consequential for what the boundary means in experience.

Myelination determines conduction velocity and temporal fidelity; unmyelinated fibers conduct slowly, disperse in time, and converge heavily, with some twenty-two axons to a single Schwann cell within a Remak bundle. 43 A myelinated afferent delivers a temporally precise and spatially specific signal.

text.text: An unmyelinated afferent field delivers an integrated one.
The precision with which a facial expression can be specified and the diffuseness of a gut feeling are not two registers of description.
They are two conduction architectures, and the discontinuity at the diaphragm is the point at which the first is no longer available.

Supradiaphragmatic and subdiaphragmatic territories therefore differ sharply in their capacity for precise sensation and precise motor control, and they are served throughout by a continuous fine afferent field.
One sensory system, variably resolved, reporting to one integrating structure and driving two output systems of markedly different speed and specificity.
Every structural term in Polyvagal Theory is efferent: the ventral vagal complex, the dorsal vagal complex, the social engagement system, the face-heart connection.

Neuroception, which names the process on which all of them depend and from which, in the theory's own ordering, they follow, is specified functionally -a detection of safety, danger and life threat proceeding below the threshold of awareness -and has not been given a structure. 44 The absence is not an oversight, and further work will not close it.

text.text: It follows from the organization of the afferent system itself.
The efferent vagus divides into two nuclei with distinct projections, and that division is what permits a two-complex taxonomy.
The afferent vagus does not divide along any comparable line.

In vivo two-photon calcium imaging of the nucleus of the solitary tract in the mouse finds its neurons topographically organized on the basis of body position, with organ representations reflecting their physical positions within the body; stimuli arising in different organs are segregated, while different inputs from the same organ converge. 45 Single-cell profiling of vagal sensory neurons across seven organs resolves their coding into three independent dimensions -visceral organ along the rostral-caudal axis, tissue layer along the surface-lumen axis of each organ, and stimulus modality -together constituting a genetic representation of the body's internal space. 46 Both studies are in mice; the viscerotopic principle is established across species, and no comparable human mapping exists.

text.text: The vagal afferent system is a map of the body's interior, organized by location and by the kind of stimulus a receptor transduces.
Its axes are anatomical and modal.
None of them is an axis of threat.
This is the structural obstacle.
Safety, danger and life threat are not positions in an organ-bytissue-layer-by-modality coordinate system; they are a different kind of thing altogether.
Safety is not a property present in the afferent signal and awaiting detection.

An anatomy of neuroception, had one been written, would have described a single viscerotopic map receiving the whole internal field -one structure, organized by body position, carrying no partition corresponding to the three conditions it is required to distinguish.
What follows is not that the organism fails to assess threat.
It is that the assessment is not delivered by the afferent system and is not located within it.
The afferent field supplies a con-tinuously updated representation of the body's internal condition; what that representation amounts to is composed, under conditions Section 6 specifies.
Assessment is distributed.

Of the four conditions under which Porges holds that Polyvagal Theory would be empirically challenged, three are stated as measures of output: that ventral vagal activity should increase rather than withdraw during defensive immobilization; that robust social engagement should occur without ventral vagal regulation; that myelination of the nucleus ambiguus should fail to coincide with the emergence of respiratory sinus arrhythmia. 3 This is a consequence of the gap identified in this section.

text.text: A theory can be tested only where it has structure, and the structure is all at the efferent end.
The conditions are written in the vocabulary of the motor system because there is nothing at the afferent end to write them about.
At its core, the Autonomics model proposes that autonomic state cannot be explained by neural circuitry alone.

Whereas Polyvagal Theory describes autonomic state as the interaction between neuroception (the perception of safety, danger, or life threat) and the neural pathways recruited in response, the present model adds a third variable: the pervading neurochemistry in which that circuitry operates.

Accordingly, autonomic state is determined by three interacting factors: 47 (1) autonomic temperature (Porges' neuroception), (2) the autonomic system that is primarily recruited -the Connection System (PVT calls this ventral vagal, Autonomics alters its neuro-anatomical boundaries), the Movement System (sympathetic), or the Grounding System (PVT calls this dorsal vagal, Autonomics alters its neuro-anatomical boundaries) -and (3) the pervading neurochemistry acting on that circuitry.

text.text: These moment-to-moment interactions occur against the background of each individual's accumulated allostatic load (conditioning history), which shapes how the nervous system responds over time.
Where the system is conditioned to enter shutdown directly the mobilized state is skipped entirely.
A sequence that follows from the chemistry admits exceptions where the chemistry differs.
An ordering intrinsic to the circuitry does not.
Section 4 establishes that bradycardia under life-threat requires both terms; what remains to be said here is why the circuitry alone cannot supply it.
The Grounding System is active throughout ordinary life: it is not merely recruited in response to life-threat.

It participates in digestion, visceral regulation, and other restorative functions. 17, 48, 49 Its presence alone even during neurocepted lifethreat cannot explain the profound slowing of the heart observed during shutdown.

text.text: In health-creating states, Connection, Movement, and Grounding all provide input to the sinoatrial node together.
Under neuroception of danger, Connection's cardioinhibitory brake lifts (the vagal brake), and sympathetic tone accelerates the heart unopposed by Connection -this is fight-or-flight physiology.

In contradistinction to the autonomic state hierarchy demarcated by PVT, Autonomics asserts that the only autonomic condition in which a single autonomic neurological system stands alone is life-threat, and it stands alone by elimination of the other two, not by exclusive recruitment.

Thus, autonomic state is determined by the changing balance among interacting systems, not by the activation of a single pathway. 50 That pervading neurochemistry is a determining variable in autonomic state is advanced here on three grounds independent of any one mechanism: the demonstration, available since 1946, that a system's chemistry and its neurology are separable; the two-pole constraint, which shows why the field's present neurochemical model cannot represent the alternative; and the single decoupling Polyvagal Theory itself performed in 2001.
