text.text: It is consistent with over a decade of clinical observation across thousands of clients at Hearth Science, where the Autonomics model was developed.
The category error diagnosed in Section 3 is not confined to the bradycardia dispute.
It is the same error that has compromised the Autonomic Ladder as Porges' own model evolved between 2011 and 2023.
The third variable is not an addition to the model.
It is the dimension in which the states under dispute are separated.
The Ladder's earliest form yielded four pure states -social engagement, fight, flight, and dorsal vagal shutdown -each reliant on a single autonomic system under a single neuroceptive condition.
By 2020, three hybrid states had been added -play, intimacy, and tonic immobility -each recruiting multiple autonomic systems at once (30).
By 2023, appease and placate had been added.
As Polyvagal Theory expanded to incorporate additional clinical phenomena, it increasingly required autonomic states that no longer fit its original one-system/one-state hierarchy.
For example, Play demonstrates that Movement-system recruitment does not necessarily imply a fight-orflight neurochemical state.
Similarly, appease and placate demonstrate that Connection-system circuitry can remain active under danger and life threat.
Finally, intimacy demonstrates that Grounding-system activity is compatible with safety.

Each addition to the Ladder since 2011 is, in retrospect, a place where the neurochemistry/neurology conflation surfaced and was accommodated locally -a new box added to the taxonomy -without the underlying conflation itself being addressed.

A second phenomenon falls outside the four conditions altogether, and is the more consequential for that reason.
Shutdown entered without antecedent mobilization resolves directly into connection, without passing through activation at all.
This is not a passage the Autonomic Ladder permits: a ladder entails sequential traversal, and that is what makes it a ladder.
The two-route account given in Section 4 explains why the transition occurs.

Where no mobilization was mounted on the way in, none is revealed on the way out, and the state reorganizes under sufficient neuroception of safety and affiliative chemistry rather than discharging an activation it never carried. 51 The observation is clinical, and its counter-instance is specifiable: a presentation entered directly in which the transition to connection cannot be made without passing through activation.

text.text: That the same circuitry returns to connection by two different routes depending on the chemistry under which it was engaged is not among the conditions Polyvagal Theory names as falsifying, because all four are stated in terms of which system is active rather than the chemistry under which it operates.
Yet the developers of a theory are not necessarily the sole authority on the complete grounds for its falsification.
The examples discussed above illustrate a broader point developed in Section 4.

If autonomic function depends on both neural circuitry and neurochemical context, then a model that considers only circuitry may generate incorrect predictions whenever the same neural pathways operate under different neurochemical conditions.
The present model therefore makes a narrower claim than either Polyvagal Theory or its critics.
It does not seek to resolve questions concerning comparative neuroanatomy or vertebrate evolution.
It declines those questions because its claims do not require their answers, not because the answers are unavailable.
On respiratory sinus arrhythmia it makes one claim and no more: that in the states this paper describes the index is not merely confounded but, where breathing has stopped, undefined.
It proposes that neurochemical context is an independent determinant of autonomic state and that this additional variable generates physiological predictions not produced by existing models.
Those predictions can, in principle, be tested directly in living human subjects using contemporary physiological measurements.

The dispute between Grossman and Porges has persisted for two decades not because either has reasoned carelessly, but because both have worked within a conceptual framework that treats neural circuitry as the primary determinant of autonomic state.
Within that framework, the disagreement cannot be resolved.

Grossman's physiological observations and Porges' clinical observations can both be correct while leading to incompatible conclusions because the shared model lacks a mechanism for distinguishing the physiological consequences of the same neural circuitry operating under different neurochemical conditions, specified by neuroceptive conditions.
The present paper proposes that neurochemical context is this missing explanatory variable: the third dimension of autonomic state (First dimension, neuroception.
Second dimension, recruited neurology).

In this account, what Grossman refers to as 'stress-related immobilization of emotional freezing or dissociation' is both under-specified relative to Porges' terminology, which reflects differentiation between tonic immobility and shutdown (see Figure 3), such that there is fundamental confusion about which terms refer to which states, and is furthermore unable to be effectively differentiated across the dimensions that determine it beyond neuroception and the recruited neural pathways: namely the neurochemical environment in which those pathways operate.

text.text: Porges has, himself, under-specified in the Polyvagal model the neurochemical conditions for shutdown.
Grossman, in asserting that the dorsal vagus does not reliably produce bradycardia, is correct: it will not produce it absent the neuroception of life-threat and the presence of endogenous opioids.
Shutdown, like all autonomic states, thus has a neuroceptive, a neurological, and a neurochemical signature.

The assertion of untenability therefore fails for the specific reason that Grossman would have to demonstrate that shutdown did not obtain under those three simultaneous conditions, which he has not done.
For that matter, neither has Porges, because PVT is missing this dimension of state construction.
It is not simply that PVT fails to cleanly differentiate play, appease, placate, intimacy, and tonic immobility by the existing rule-based structure of its own taxonomy.
Rather, these states are the visible edge of the missing dimension distinguished by variable pervading neurochemistry.

The inclusion of this neurochemical dimension generates a greatly expanded state taxonomy that more accurately maps to clinical observation, obviates the autonomic ladder, and generates specific physiological predictions that neither Polyvagal Theory nor its current critiques produce.

With respect to the Porges/Grossman controversy specifically, it predicts opposite cardiac outcomes under life-threat depending upon whether a pervading opioid chemistry is present or absent, and a respiratory signature that distinguishes the two states without recourse to the heart.
The contribution of this paper is therefore not a new account of comparative neuroanatomy or vertebrate evolution.
Where it does make an anatomical claim, that claim concerns human tissue measured directly rather than lineages inferred across species.

Nor is the contribution a general defense or rejection of respiratory sinus arrhythmia as a physiological marker, beyond the specific finding that it cannot be computed in a state without a respiratory frequency.
It is a more specific claim: that autonomic state cannot be fully understood from neural circuitry alone.

Neuroception, neural circuitry and neurochemical context jointly determine physiological expression, and separating those variables transforms a long-standing conceptual dispute into experimentally testable hypotheses capable of being tested and resolved in living persons.
Two findings established here survive the outcome of the dispute entirely.

The partition of the vagus at the respiratory diaphragm has been argued for twenty years on comparative grounds -the phylogenetic status of myelinated against unmyelinated cardioinhibitory fiber, the derivation of vagal control from cardiorespiratory synchrony in fish -and it requires none of them.
Electron microscopy of human vagal tissue locates the discontinuity directly, confined to the myelinated population, with large-calibre fiber present above the diaphragm and absent below.

This is the single point in the entire controversy at which a comparative argument is replaced by a direct human measurement, and no position in the controversy touches it: Grossman contests the phylogeny and the measurement, Porges defends the phylogeny, and the boundary is established by neither route, because neither party has had an instrument that registers it.

What the boundary marks is not two systems but two conduction architectures, and the clinical difference between the precision with which a face can be read and the diffuseness of a visceral sense is a difference in available resolution rather than in register of description.
Porges' central anatomical intuition is therefore vindicated on grounds he did not have.
What is vindicated is the partition and not the taxonomy erected upon it, and the partition does not fall if the taxonomy does.

This partition is, furthermore, of the afferent architecture, which, though composing the numerical majority of autonomic fibers (73.9-80+%), has been under-specified and insufficiently visualized, resolved, mapped and differentiated throughout the history of autonomic science: surely ironic given that the interoceptive capabilities arising from its sensory conduction architecture are the primary living intelligence of these systems.

Grossman et al.'s expertise notwithstanding, Polyvagal Theory cannot be definitively demonstrated untenable unless testable hypotheses can demonstrate that its predictions fail to produce the neurophysiological outcomes it predicts in living subjects under life-threat, with the recruited neurology of shutdown, and its pervading neurochemistry.
Nor can it be vindicated, Porges' expertise notwithstanding, except by the same: a demonstration that its premises obtain in living subjects.

The present paper provides a concrete, experimentally testable series of predictions that can be used to adjudicate what has until now been an unresolvable, stasisinducing, and ultimately academic debate unsettling the field and further separating academic neuroscience from its application in clinical praxis.
If these predictions are supported, the implications extend beyond the specific controversy surrounding dorsal vagal shutdown.
They suggest that autonomic state is more accurately understood as an emergent property of interacting neural and neurochemical processes than as the fixed function of particular anatomical pathways.
Whether this account proves correct is ultimately an empirical question.
The scope of the present paper is not to settle that question, but to formulate it in a way that can now be tested.

Porges did not present the asymmetry as established: his own text calls the more specific peripheral mechanism "this speculation," and offers as its sole supporting evidence vasopressin's association with motion-sickness nausea (p. 139), a correlational finding rather than a demonstration of the proposed DMX pathway.
He did not return to the claim.

The 2007 commentary on heart rate variability research, written to answer a critique by Grossman and Taylor in the same special issue, addresses vagal tone, respiratory sinus arrhythmia and the vagal brake at length, and does not mention vasopressin, oxytocin, or the neurochemical conditioning of the dorsal vagal complex in any context.
The most recent publications retain the receptor anatomy and drop the mechanism.

Porges (2025b) restates dorsal vagal shutdown twice -that individuals may oscillate between sympathetic mobilization and dorsal vagal shutdown without reliable access to the ventral vagal complex (p. 174), and that sympathetic mobilization and dorsal vagal immobilization are critical for survival in the face of threat (p. 176) -without mentioning vasopressin in either passage or anywhere else in the paper; its single AVP reference concerns unrelated transcriptomic gene expression in the nucleus ambiguus.

Porges (2025a), published the same year, does discuss vasopressin, identifying Avpr1a receptors as more prominently expressed in the dorsal vagal complex and NTS, but assigns them a sympathetic function only: Avpr1a activation promotes autonomic mobilization in response to perceived threat, and vasopressin shifts the system toward sympathetic activation under threat and may sustain defensive hypervigilance.
That paper explains shutdown by Jacksonian dissolution rather than by any named neurochemical trigger.
The receptor sits in the dorsal complex; the function assigned to it does not.
Two independent treatments converge on the same absence.

Lanius et al. (2018), building an opioid-based account of dissociative shutdown, cite the 2011 book for the proposition that immobilization and death feigning occur through activation of the dorsal vagal complex and its inhibitory inputs to the heart -anatomy only, with no reference to vasopressin, in a paper whose stated purpose is to supply the neurochemistry the anatomical model lacks.

Grossman et al. (2026), citing the 2025b passages above by page number, state that the concept of dorsal vagal shutdown in humans is completely without evidence (p. 104), addressing only the anatomical claim.

The most direct test of whether the formulation remains in use is the 2026 review Porges co-authored, whose subject is the neuropeptide regulation of the brain-heart axis and which treats oxytocin and vasopressin at length. 18 It does not reinstate the 2001 mechanism; it reverses half of it.

text.text: Vasopressin is assigned to the sympathetic limb -V1a activation increasing sympathetic tone, promoting vasoconstriction, and amplifying hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal activity under social threat -and is nowhere connected to dorsal motor nucleus potentiation, to bradycardia, or to immobilization.

Oxytocin retains its dorsal site, acting at the nucleus of the solitary tract and the dorsal motor nucleus, but is assigned baroreflex sensitivity and vagal control rather than fear-free immobilization.

The dorsal vagal complex is characterized throughout as a visceromotor and cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, a characterization the review repeatedly distinguishes from respiratory sinus arrhythmia and high-frequency heart rate variability; immobilization appears once in the review, in a hedged clause stating that dorsal pathways may mediate immobilization responses under extreme threat.
What survives is the position without the mechanism.

The review retains the placement the 2001 formulation was written to explain -the dorsal vagal complex predominating at high challenge intensity, in states associated with physiological shutdown and overload -while the peptide that was to produce it has been reassigned to the opposite limb of the hierarchy and no replacement is named.
The change is not noted, the 2001 mechanism is not cited, and the two positions are not reconciled.
The pattern across a quarter-century is therefore not retraction.

The proposed role of vasopressin in dorsal vagal shutdown was introduced once, in 2001, hedged as speculation and supported only by a correlational finding; it is absent from every subsequent treatment of the same phenomenon; and in the most recent, the peptide is doing the opposite work.
Neither those building on the theory nor those criticising it engage the mechanism in its original form, because neither had occasion to encounter it in the later work.
The hypothesis was not withdrawn.
It was left standing while the claim it was written to support was carried forward without it.

The clinical observations reported in this section derive from two bodies of work, and the distinction bears on what each supports.
The broader is more than two decades of practice with several thousand people, conducted individually, in the presence of trained practitioners, and in public demonstration before groups.
The narrower is the Autonomics Clinic, established in 2020, a boutique practice taking approximately seventy cases by referral and application and selecting for complexity and research interest.
Clients are adults between eighteen and eightysix.

The clinic excludes complex chronic illness, including fibromyalgia, myalgic encephalomyelitis, chronic Lyme disease, autoimmune conditions and mast cell activation syndrome; active psychosis and Axis II presentations; the autism spectrum; and current use of psychotropic medication, including antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, antidepressants and sleep medication.

The last exclusion is methodologically consequential here, since the states described were observed in adults not taking centrally active medication and are therefore not pharmacologically confounded.

The same exclusions bound what the observations generalize to.States are identified by direct obser-vation of expressed physiology rather than by self-report: breathing rate and depth, muscle tone, posture, gesture, vocal prosody, eye gaze, pupillary response, capillary dilation, position of the head on the neck, the surfacing of reflexive and protective motor gestures, and the presence or absence of interoceptive sensation across regions of the body.
The method is observational and skilled rather than instrumented, and it includes a component of trained intuition refined across several thousand sessions.
Its calibration is nonetheless testable in the way a tracker's is: a state transition is predicted, and it either occurs or it does not.
Where a person arrives without sensation in a region and leaves with it, the intervention produced a change, and the prediction that it would is borne out or it is not.
Assignment of the two routes into shutdown is made before any exit is observed, from the history and from the physiology concurrently.

A specific life-threat event with active defense already in progress, a triggering circumstance disproportionate to the state it produces, shutdown as a habitual rather than an occasioned configuration, and the presence or absence of a rigid high-tone phase preceding collapse are each available at the outset.
The exit is therefore a test of the assignment rather than its basis.
The claims differ in strength.

That attentional contact with a localized shutdown is accompanied by cessation of breathing is exceptionless across both bodies of work and is observed daily in current practice; its counter-instance is specifiable and has not been encountered.

That the presence or absence of air hunger governs which intervention the state will accept is weaker: it has been observed consistently but has not been the specific object of attention, and is offered as a provisional regularity rather than an established one.

Air hunger is read from the physiology rather than reported -its presence appears as struggle, its absence as indifference -and it is the same observation from which the affective signature described above is drawn.
Both regularities were discerned retrospectively, as patterns across accumulated clinical experience, and subsequently confirmed in ongoing practice.
Neither was logged prospectively under a protocol.
What counts as the return of breathing requires specification, because a volitional breath and an endogenous one are not the same event.
A person in shutdown can force a breath mechanically, and doing so does not alter the state.

What these observations concern is the breath arriving without being driven -the respiratory rhythm resuming rather than ventilation being produced -which is why the clinical instruction is to release what prevents breathing rather than to breathe.
The distinction corresponds to the separation of volitional from automatic respiratory control, and only the latter is at issue.
Everyone seen in the clinic signs an extensive consent to treat.
No individual described in this paper is identified by anything other than clustered symptomatology, and no identifying information appears.
Three things are not claimed.
Nothing here establishes prevalence, the population being selected and small.

Nothing here establishes mechanism: clinical observation is strong evidence for the existence of these presentations, for their co-occurrence, for their phenomenology, and for the discriminations being ones an observer reliably makes, and it is not evidence for the chemistry proposed to underlie them, which is advanced separately and is severable from them.

And the efficacy of the intervention, whatever it establishes about the intervention, is not offered as evidence that the mechanistic account is correct, since an intervention can succeed for reasons its explanation gets wrong.
Each observation has an instrumented form it has not yet taken.

The apnoea and the regularization are measurable with a respiratory band; whether ventilation in the deepest presentations falls to zero or only to low amplitude requires that band with concurrent pulse oximetry; and the interval between the return of air hunger and the first endogenous breath is a recordable latency.
None of these has been done yet.
